name: Assistive Technology and Communication
title: Assistive Technology and Communication
answer: Assistive technology can open education to students with disabilities, but only when the right tool is matched to the right student and the adults around them are trained to use it. AI can help teams search and compare options, yet the choice stays with the assistive technology specialist, the family, and the student. The most common barrier is not the technology itself but training, information, and accessibility.

sections.body: Assistive technology covers tools that give students with disabilities access to learning and communication, from symbol based communication apps to braille translation and accessible graphing. The problem it solves is exclusion: without the right tool, students are shut out of grade level content and of expressing themselves. Matching a tool to a student is a skill, not a purchase, and AI can assist teams by searching vendor catalogs and comparing options. The decision itself belongs to the people who know the student, namely the assistive technology specialist, the family, and the student. This keeps the tool tied to the student's actual needs rather than to what is easiest to buy.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day use, a student who cannot rely on speech may use an augmentative and alternative communication device such as Proloquo2Go, which builds messages from symbols and word prediction. AI powered word prediction can speed that communication up considerably, but the vocabulary, symbols, and settings are chosen with the speech pathologist and family so the device reflects the student's own voice. For students who are blind, Desmos accessibility features let them explore graphs through sound, and braille translation software converts materials, with a teacher of the visually impaired checking the output. These tools make grade level content reachable, and they depend on trained staff to work well. Training should extend to the student as well, so they can use their tools independently.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. A review of 31 studies found that assistive technology increases inclusion and access for students with disabilities, and that the main barriers are teacher training, information, and accessibility (Fernandez-Batanero, 2022). The text also names training as the barrier the research mentions most often, and notes that a district buying assistive technology without training teachers will see devices sitting in drawers. No other studies or figures are given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are practical and human. A district that buys devices without training the adults who work with the student will find those devices unused, so budgets for assistive technology should include training for every adult who works with the student. The vocabulary, symbols, and settings on a communication device must be chosen with the speech pathologist and family so the device reflects the student's own voice, and braille output should be checked by a teacher of the visually impaired. AI can help search catalogs and compare options, but the choice stays with the assistive technology specialist, the family, and the student. These tools depend on trained staff to use them well, and the student should be trained too so they can use their tools independently.
